Marlow Bates & Tamir Stanfield on "The Wire" Based on Them, Selling Drugs in Baltimore (Part 1)

--------
In this VladTV interview, Marlow Bates and Tamir Stanfield, real-life half brothers from West Baltimore, discuss the 1980s heroin era that helped inspire the Marlo Stanfield character on HBO’s *The Wire*. Now free after decades in prison on murder convictions tied to that period, they reflect on growing up in a crowded Baltimore household, early exposure to heroin, guns, and street life, and how family dynamics shaped their paths.

The conversation covers their move from selling weed as teens to entering Baltimore’s drug trade, expanding through housing projects like Murphy Homes, and building connections that reached New York, Philly, and Jersey. They also speak on Little Melvin Williams, Lewisburg prison, the city’s interconnected street networks, and claims about police tactics and legal cases from that era.

A firsthand look at Baltimore history, street politics, and the real stories linked to *The Wire*.

Charleston White sits down with VladTV to discuss the fallout from interviews he says were pulled after pressure from T.I., naming Big Bank, DJ Akademiks, Funny Marco, 85 South and others. White reflects on how the situation affected him personally, saying it changed the way he viewed artists he once admired, including T.I., Boosie and Jeezy, and pushed him to become more aggressive in his online persona.

In this VladTV interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez recalls sharing federal prison space with George Jung, better known as Boston George, and challenges key parts of the Hollywood version seen in *Blow* starring Johnny Depp. Dominguez says Jung was connected to Carlos Lehder early on, before Lehder became a major Medellín Cartel figure tied to Norman’s Cay in the Bahamas and Pablo Escobar’s cocaine pipeline. He describes Jung’s first alleged Colombia trip, suitcase smuggling through customs, and why he believes the movie overstated George’s role, including claims of meeting Escobar. The conversation also covers Lehder’s extradition to the United States, Jung becoming a government witness, prison politics, and the difference between cartel mythmaking and what Dominguez says he heard firsthand. A grounded look at true crime history, federal cases, and the real people behind one of America’s most famous drug-smuggling stories.

Lil Jungle Boy sits down with Vlad to discuss the fallout from his viral 2022 Soft White Underbelly interview, a Super Bowl–week arrest, and the legal trouble that followed. He addresses allegations tied to robbery, arson, residential burglary, stolen firearms and an involuntary manslaughter charge, while avoiding details on matters he says remain unresolved. Lil Jungle Boy also recalls being detained with ghost gun kits in his backpack, placed in a police car, kicking out a window, and being shot by officers while running away in handcuffs.

Now off parole, he says he’s focused on legal work, staying out of the streets, and building a gang prevention effort for younger people influenced by rap videos, guns, jewelry and street culture. He also reflects on violence in hip-hop, including MO3’s freeway killing and the ongoing trial, warning that the lifestyle often ends in prison, paranoia or death.

In this VladTV interview, Rene “Boxer” Enriquez reflects on how he was groomed inside prison before becoming a made member of the Mexican Mafia in 1985 at just 23 years old. Enriquez describes conversations with figures including Black Dan Borella, Raymond Welsh, and a high-ranking member from Artesia, explaining how sponsorship, prison politics, and reputation shaped his path into the organization.  

He recalls the moment he says he was voted in, signaled through the “Black Hand of Death,” and how it felt like the peak of his criminal identity at the time. Enriquez also discusses the Mexican Mafia’s dormancy during a period of state indictments, SHU housing, isolation from Nuestra Familia members, and tensions involving BGF. The interview offers a firsthand look at California prison gang structure, loyalty, and the rules that governed life behind bars in the 1980s.

--------
In this VladTV interview, Tito “TJ” Dominguez recounts the high-risk shift from marijuana runs between Miami, the Bahamas and Colombia to cocaine transportation in the early 1980s. After a botched airdrop left him owing $800,000 to Colombian traffickers from La Guajira, Dominguez says he was kidnapped in Kendall, south of Miami, and given 24 hours to pay. His solution: fly a Beechcraft-style plane he called “Gigi,” the “Gray Ghost,” to move 450 kilos of cocaine — an event he says later appeared in one of his indictments.

Dominguez also describes meeting Pablo Escobar, Gustavo, and Escobar’s Miami representative Ramirez, negotiating kilo rates, using radios and code names like “Ciclón,” and securing a Bahamas airport through bribery. The conversation offers a firsthand look at drug smuggling logistics, cartel pressure, and the dangerous line between marijuana trafficking and the cocaine trade.

In this VladTV interview, Lil Jungle Boy reflects on returning home in March 2020 as Drakeo the Ruler’s post-prison momentum was rising and the controversial track “Ingleweird” spread through Los Angeles. Speaking as someone tied to Inglewood and South Central street politics, he says many homies disliked the record, but argues that backlash often follows when artists speak on uncomfortable realities inside the culture. Vlad and Lil Jungle Boy also discuss Drakeo’s later killing backstage at a concert, the reaction in Blood neighborhoods, and why he views much of the public conversation as hearsay. The conversation shifts to Big U’s federal case and the alleged studio killing of Rashawn, whom Lil Jungle Boy identifies as his cousin. He reacts to the allegations while stressing there is “more to the story” and that facts still matter.
